title: bug: rollback and migrate_down guard the same environment on two different streams, so both can move its schema at once
description:
MEASURED at HEAD ac799ed8 on 2026-09-11 by architect-1c0fef54. Filed as the successor task-705977238f794b2cadb5c1dcdb98d6bd's own scope fence authorizes: "Concurrency exclusion is NOT in this row - it is a separate mechanism and would breach the size caps. File it as a successor if this row's plan shows the seam." It did, twice over.

THE DEFECT. Three commands can move ONE environment's schema, and they guard it in three mutually blind ways:

    rollback-command.ts:140      `rollback-environment:<sha256(projectId, environment)>`
    migrate-down-admission.ts:39 `migrate-down-environment:<sha256(...)>`
    deploy-command.ts:140        no per-environment guard at all; aggregateIdFor(request, null) is the PROJECT stream

So a `deployment.migrate_down` reverting a batch and a `deployment.rollback` restoring a dump can be admitted against the same environment at the same moment. Each checks a stream the other never touches. Both then write to the same database. Neither refuses, and both record a receipt saying it succeeded.

THE PROTOCOLS ARE ALREADY IDENTICAL, which is what makes this small. Both use odd-means-reserved parity on a private per-environment stream, both read it with `store.getAggregateVersion`, both reserve with an event in the admission commit and release in the terminal. rollback-command.ts:237-247 and migrate-down-admission.ts:105-116 are the same shape with different prefixes. Unifying them is a shared derivation, not a new mechanism.

NO NEW VOCABULARY IS NEEDED. Each command keeps its own code when it finds the guard odd: rollback answers DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_IN_PROGRESS, migrate_down answers MIGRATE_DOWN_IN_PROGRESS. An operator sees the code of the command they issued, which is what the closed code-to-layer maps already pin. Do not add a code.

THE UPGRADE HAZARD, which the plan must decide deliberately. A request admitted BEFORE this change reserved the old stream and stored its guardVersion in the intent decision. Its recovery would release that version against the NEW stream, where it never reserved, so the expectedVersion leg refuses and the request can never finish. Either derive the guard id from the intent record so an in-flight request keeps its original stream, or refuse such a request with a clear code, or state why the window is acceptable. Whichever is chosen, say it in the module header and pin it with an arm.

SCOPE FENCE. This row unifies ROLLBACK and MIGRATE_DOWN only. Fencing `deployment.deploy` is a separate and larger change: a deploy holds its environment across build, migrate, candidate start and health polling, so taking a schema guard for that whole span changes how long an environment is unavailable to other operators. File it as a successor to this row, not inside it.

RELATED, ALREADY CLOSED, DO NOT REDO. qa-77a9823a recorded a walk-order hazard on task-705977238f794b2cadb5c1dcdb98d6bd at 11:10: a deploy interleaving inside a rollback's window makes a dump walk ordered by deploy receipts pick the restored schema. task-aa6f9af4735449a5b5e098f52f78fc54 closes the WALK half by ordering on the decision ledger's commit position, and carries an arm for exactly that interleaving. This row is about the FENCE, which is still absent: the walk now answers safely about a race that nothing prevents.

THE LEAF: apps/daemon/src/deployment/environment-schema-guard.ts plus its one-line bridge environment-schema-guard.js containing exactly `export * from "./environment-schema-guard.ts";` (every sibling .ts in this directory has one; a missing bridge breaks the .js specifiers the slice imports by).

It exports IDS ONLY - no reserve, no release, no store access:
  - `environmentSchemaGuardId(projectId, environment)`: the ONE stream both schema-moving commands guard. Pick a single prefix and a single hashed shape and say in a comment which of the two old shapes you kept and why.
  - `legacyRollbackGuardId(projectId, environment)` and `legacyMigrateDownGuardId(projectId, environment)`: the exact pre-change derivations, byte-for-byte, kept so an in-flight request admitted before this change can still be released. Mark them clearly as compatibility-only and not to be used for new reservations.

THE HEADER CARRIES THE INVARIANT, because it is the whole point of the module: one environment has one schema, so the commands that MOVE that schema share one parity. State the two that do (rollback restore, migrate_down revert) and that deploy is deliberately NOT among them yet, naming the successor as future work rather than pretending it is covered.

Also state the consequence the reader will otherwise hit as a surprise: both commands deliberately leave the guard ODD when an effect's outcome is unknown, and after unification that blocks the other command too. That is correct - the schema's state is unknown, so nothing else may move it - and recovery is unaffected because each command reads its guardVersion from its own intent rather than re-checking parity.
implementationPlan.note:
THE LEAF LANDED. 108 lines, ids only — no reserve, no release, no store import. Its one runtime import is node:crypto.

THREE EXPORTS:
  environmentSchemaGuardId(projectId, environment) -> `environment-schema:${sha256(JSON.stringify({projectId, environment}))}`
  legacyRollbackGuardId    -> `rollback-environment:${sha256(JSON.stringify({projectId, environment}))}`      (compat only)
  legacyMigrateDownGuardId -> `migrate-down-environment:${sha256(JSON.stringify([projectId, environment]))}`  (compat only)

WHICH OLD SHAPE I KEPT AND WHY, as the step asked: the ROLLBACK's OBJECT `{projectId, environment}`,
over migrate_down's positional ARRAY. A named-key shape says what each component is at the one place
a reader can check it; a positional one silently means something else the day a third component is
appended. The PREFIX is new — `environment-schema:` names what is guarded rather than which command
guards it, and a new prefix also guarantees no unified id collides with either legacy stream, so an
old in-flight request's parity and a new one's can never be confused.

THE LEGACY DERIVATIONS ARE BYTE-FOR-BYTE, and I proved it rather than eyeballing it. Both production
encoders are the same function — rollback-command.ts:44 `encoder.encode(JSON.stringify(value))`,
migrate-down-admission.ts:13 `new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(value))` — so the leaf's own
`digest` reproduces both exactly. Sample for projectId "p", environment "production":
  rollback legacy: rollback-environment:7ab5f2e87f0908f4d29cdd2e353043efe3bd15c3e2592ae114299c53052620bc
  migdown  legacy: migrate-down-environment:38cc8e7beb9d5768c8ed2ed84ed4bf566b5a4da03a6933f107c644449125bd07
  unified        : environment-schema:7ab5f2e87f0908f4d29cdd2e353043efe3bd15c3e2592ae114299c53052620bc
Note the unified id's HASH equals the rollback legacy's (same shape) and only the prefix differs —
that is the shape choice being visible, and it is why the prefix had to change rather than stay.

THE HEADER CARRIES FOUR THINGS, all of them load-bearing:
 1. The invariant — one environment has one schema, so the commands that move it share one parity —
    naming the two that do (rollback restore, migrate_down revert).
 2. That `deployment.deploy` is DELIBERATELY not among them yet, with the reason (a deploy holds its
    environment across build, migrate, candidate start and health polling, so fencing it changes how
    long an environment is unavailable — an operator-visible product decision, not a bug fix) and
    named as a successor. It says plainly that this module NARROWS the hole and does not close it.
 3. The surprise: both commands leave the guard ODD on an uncertain effect, and that now blocks the
    OTHER command too. Stated as correct — the schema's state is unknown, so nothing else may move
    it — with the note that recovery is unaffected because each command reads its guardVersion from
    its own intent rather than re-checking parity.
 4. THE UPGRADE HAZARD AND THE CHOSEN BEHAVIOUR (DoD item 6), in writing: a pre-change request STILL
    COMPLETES, ON ITS ORIGINAL STREAM. Every intent from now on records the guard id it reserved; an
    intent carrying no id is by construction pre-change, so recovery falls back to that command's
    legacy derivation and releases the stream it really took. The header also states the RESIDUAL
    window — while such a request is in flight it holds only its legacy stream, so it does not
    exclude the other command; the window is bounded by that one request's lifetime — and why the
    alternative (replaying old guard events onto the new id) was rejected: it rewrites durable
    history to fix a transient window. Steps 6's arms pin the chosen behaviour in BOTH directions.

The `.js` bridge is the exact one-liner every sibling has: `export * from "./environment-schema-guard.ts";`.
Nothing imports the leaf yet — steps 4 and 5 wire the two call sites. No test run in this step; the
